title: Life, liberty, conviction, education, arrest — Articles 20–22 and 21A

content.overview: Article 20 protects persons against ex post facto criminal law, double jeopardy, and compulsion to be a witness against oneself. Article 21 says no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. The existing overview records that, after Maneka, that procedure must be fair, just and reasonable; that proposition is not expanded into a new holding here. Article 21A requires the State to provide free and compulsory education to children from six to fourteen years in the manner the State may by law determine. Article 22 deals with arrest and detention: grounds and legal consultation, production before a magistrate within twenty-four hours, and a separate regime for preventive detention.
content.study: Separate conviction protections in Article 20, deprivation of liberty in Article 21, education in Article 21A, and arrest procedure in Article 22. Do not use Article 22's punitive-arrest rules as if they were the preventive-detention code.

sections.heading: Article 21 after Maneka
sections.body: Procedure established by law must be fair, just and reasonable. Do not treat Article 21 as a free-standing damages statute.

sections.heading: Article 20
sections.body: Three protections: no ex post facto conviction/greater penalty; no double jeopardy; no compelled self-incrimination.

learningObjectives: State Article 21 and Article 21A without inventing a due-process ratio.
Separate ordinary arrest safeguards from preventive detention in Article 22.
enhancement.definition: Articles 20, 21, 21A and 22 protect persons in criminal conviction, life and personal liberty, elementary education, and arrest or preventive detention.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Article 21 is person-wide and procedure-based. Article 20 is criminal-conviction specific. Article 22 adds arrest safeguards and a distinct preventive-detention procedure.
essentialIngredients: Article 20 limited to criminal accusation or conviction
Article 21 deprivation by procedure established by law
Article 21A age band of six to fourteen
Article 22 grounds, counsel and twenty-four-hour production for ordinary arrest
Preventive detention clauses applied only to that detention
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Article 20(1) bars conviction except for violation of a law in force at the time of the act, and bars a greater penalty than the law then allowed. Article 20(2) bars prosecution and punishment for the same offence more than once. Article 20(3) bars compulsion of an accused to be a witness against himself. Article 21 uses person and procedure established by law. The fair, just and reasonable reading is already noted in the topic and remains a case-law gate. Article 21A is a State duty for children aged six to fourteen. Article 22(1) and (2) give grounds of arrest, a right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of the arrested person's choice, and production before the nearest magistrate within twenty-four hours excluding the journey. Clauses (4) to (7) are the preventive-detention code: advisory board, communication of grounds, representation, and parliamentary prescription of maximum period. An enemy alien or a person detained under a preventive-detention law is excluded from clauses (1) and (2) by clause (3).
examples: A penalty is increased after the act and applied to that act. Article 20(1) is the plea.
An arrested person is not produced before a magistrate within twenty-four hours. Article 22(2) applies if the detention is not preventive detention.
A child of eight is denied free elementary education. Article 21A is the clause, not Article 19.
enhancement.problemApplication: Classify the complaint as conviction, deprivation of liberty, education, ordinary arrest, or preventive detention. Apply only that clause.
distinctions: Article 22(1) and (2) arrest vs clauses (4) to (7) preventive detention
Article 21 any person vs Article 19 citizens

keyTakeaways: Article 20 covers ex post facto criminal law, double jeopardy and self-incrimination.
Article 21 protects any person's life and personal liberty.
Article 21A covers ages six to fourteen.
Ordinary arrest requires grounds, counsel and production within twenty-four hours.
Preventive detention has its own clauses.

verification.note: Clause text only. Maneka is retained as a name already in the overview and is not given a new ratio.
